大傳論造化之生成，一出於無心也。蓋天地之所以大者，其機神也。知始作成，一易簡而已，何庸心哉！夫子言此，欲人法易簡也。蓋曰：大易之理，備于天地。人知天地之化大，而亦知其化之神乎？今夫功莫難於創始，非若循襲者之易爲力也。乾知大始，吾意物之仰於天者衆，而天之生之亦難矣。不知乾，健而動者也。剛決之性，當機則發，而觸之者槖籥自開；陽生之意，遇時則行，而迎之者機緘自動。物莫能禦，故始萬品之物，易猶一物也；時莫能窮，故始萬古之物，易猶…
translation_en:
"Qian knows through the easy; Kun acts through the simple."

Gu Dingchen 顧鼎臣 〔 〕
Associate Examiner, Instructor Ou 區, comments: 〔One who skillfully brings out the marvels of creation and transformation.〕
Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Zhu 諸, comments: 〔The principle of the topic is profound and abstruse, yet this composition expounds it with clarity and penetration; it truly deserves a high recommendation.〕
Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Long 龍, comments: 〔Proper in structure and lofty in tone; fresh in conception and polished in diction.〕
Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent He 何, comments: 〔It brings out the meaning of knowing through the easy and acting through the simple.〕
Examiner, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Fan 范, comments: 〔Precise, accurate, and worthy of serving as a model.〕

The Great Commentary (Dazhuan) discusses how the generation and completion of creation and transformation issue entirely without deliberate mind. For that by which Heaven and Earth are great is the marvelousness of their vital mechanism. Governing the beginnings and bringing things to completion are a matter of ease and simplicity alone—what need is there for deliberate mind! The Master spoke of this because he wished for people to model themselves on ease and simplicity.

It is as if to say: The principles of the Great Changes (Dayi) are fully present in Heaven and Earth. People know that the transformations of Heaven and Earth are great, but do they also know that their transformations are marvelous?

Now, among achievements, none is more difficult than initiating a beginning; it is not like following along in established tracks, where it is easy to exert one's strength. "Qian knows the great beginnings"—I would have thought that since the things relying upon Heaven are so numerous, for Heaven to give them birth would also be difficult. Yet one does not realize that Qian is vigorous and active. Its firm and decisive nature issues forth as soon as it meets the right moment, and for whatever comes into contact with it, the bellows opens of itself; its yang-generating impulse moves forward as soon as it encounters the right season, and for whatever meets it, the hidden mechanism stirs of itself. Nothing can withstand it; therefore, initiating the myriad varieties of things is as easy as initiating a single thing. Time cannot exhaust it; therefore, initiating the things of myriad ages is as easy as…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
一時也雖乾知其始而不自知所以始其造化
之良知乎事莫煩於代終非若造端者之執其
要也坤作成物吾意物之始於天者衆而地之
成之亦煩矣孰知坤順而靜者也虛受以爲常
不待更張而有生之朕兆已顯順從以爲職無
所專遂而衆動之胚胎自呈代天有終則萬物
之生成若矣無繁賾也承天時行則萬古之物
知斯矣無猥瑣也雖坤能作成而不自知所以
成其造化之良能乎吁總天下之物類而歸之
===
乾坤總乾坤之生成而歸之易簡然則天地之
道果一言而可盡也與抑論曰易曰簡就乾坤
而立名名雖二實則一也所謂無心是也然聖
賢法天地猶曰有心而無爲何哉聖賢雖有心
而與太虛同體無自私用智之擾而有順應不
滯之便是亦無心而已矣是故心貴虛實則道
無所居心貴一兩則道無所適此聖賢所以貴
易簡之學也
書
punctuated:
一時也。雖乾知其始，而不自知所以始，其造化之良知乎！事莫煩於代終，非若造端者之執其要也。坤作成物，吾意物之始於天者衆，而地之成之亦煩矣。孰知坤順而靜者也，虛受以爲常，不待更張，而有生之朕兆已顯；順從以爲職，無所專遂，而衆動之胚胎自呈。代天有終，則萬物之生成若矣，無繁賾也；承天時行，則萬古之物知斯矣，無猥瑣也。雖坤能作成，而不自知所以成，其造化之良能乎！吁！總天下之物類而歸之乾坤，總乾坤之生成而歸之易簡，然則天地之道，果一言而可盡也與！抑論曰「易」曰「簡」，就乾坤而立名，名雖二，實則一也，所謂無心是也。然聖賢法天地，猶曰有心而無爲，何哉？聖賢雖有心，而與太虛同體，無自私用智之擾，而有順應不滯之便，是亦無心而已矣。是故心貴虛，實則道無所居；心貴一，兩則道無所適。此聖賢所以貴易簡之學也。
書
translation_en:
… a single moment. Although Qian directs their beginning, it does not itself know how it begins them—is this not the innate knowledge (liangzhi) of the creative transformation?

In affairs, nothing is more troublesome than bringing things to completion on another's behalf, unlike initiating a beginning, where one simply grasps the essentials. "Kun acts to bring things to completion." I would have thought that since the things begun by Heaven are so multitude, Earth's completing them must also be troublesome. Who would know that Kun is compliant and tranquil! Taking receptive emptiness as its constant norm, it does not wait to alter course before theincipient signs of life are already manifest; taking compliant following as its duty, it claims no autonomous accomplishment of its own before the embryos of all movements naturally present themselves. Bringing things to completion on Heaven's behalf, the generation and completion of the myriad things proceed smoothly, without complexity or intricacy; acting in timely accordance with Heaven, the things of all antiquity are thus known [?], without pettiness or fragmentation. Although Kun is able to act and bring things to completion, it does not itself know how it completes them—is this not the innate ability (liangneng) of the creative transformation!

Ah! Gathering all the categories of things in the world and attributing them to Qian and Kun, and gathering the generation and completion of Qian and Kun and attributing them to the easy and the simple—then can the Way of Heaven and Earth indeed be exhausted in a single phrase! Furthermore, if we discuss the terms "easy" and "simple," the names are established with reference to Qian and Kun; although the names are two, the reality is one: it is what is called having no deliberate mind (wuxin). Yet when sages and worthies model themselves on Heaven and Earth, it is still said that they have a mind but engage in no deliberate action (wuwei)—why is this? Although sages and worthies have a mind, they share the same substance as the Great Vacuity; free from the disturbance of selfishness and cleverness, they possess the ease of responding compliantly without obstruction—this too is nothing other than having no deliberate mind. Therefore, the mind values emptiness: if it isstuffed full, the Way has nowhere to dwell; the mind values unity: if it is divided in two, the Way has nowhere to go. This is why sages and worthies value the learning of the easy and the simple.

Book of Documents (Shu)

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
惟德動天無遠弗屆滿招損謙受益時乃
天道
江文明
同考試官學正黃　批〔此題難處在於聯屬　場中作者外不相應是篇理意圓融而詞復曲〕
〔盡非邃於養者未能也宜錄以式四方〕
同考試官教授孫　批〔識高理邃發透天人〕
〔感應之妙非徒以其文已也敬服敬服〕
考試官右中允何　批〔明暢藝策〕
===
考試官左中允范　批〔文有關鍵可錄〕
大臣極言德感乎天而因明諸天道也夫德之
感通無間于天之遠也滿損謙益天且弗違而
况於人乎伯益以是贊禹也若謂至德者感應
之原盈虛者屈伸之理苗民未服蠢亦反其在
我而求端於天乎彼頑弗卽工是威不可制也
勤兵無益是力不足恃也惟夫昭德之至者非
特感人已也馨香上通于於穆雖天體至遠而
精神之昭格方所不能爲之拘非若威之有所
punctuated:
「惟德動天，無遠弗屆。滿招損，謙受益，時乃天道。」
江文明
同考試官學正黃　批：〔此題難處在於聯屬，場中作者外不相應。是篇理意圓融，而詞復曲盡，非邃於養者未能也。宜錄以式四方。〕
同考試官教授孫　批：〔識高理邃，發透天人感應之妙，非徒以其文已也。敬服，敬服！〕
考試官右中允何　批：〔明暢，藝策。〕
考試官左中允范　批：〔文有關鍵，可錄。〕
大臣極言德感乎天，而因明諸天道也。夫德之感通，無間于天之遠也。滿損謙益，天且弗違，而况於人乎？伯益以是贊禹也。若謂：至德者，感應之原；盈虛者，屈伸之理。苗民未服，蠢亦反其在我，而求端於天乎！彼頑弗卽工，是威不可制也；勤兵無益，是力不足恃也。惟夫昭德之至者，非特感人已也。馨香上通于於穆，雖天體至遠，而精神之昭格，方所不能爲之拘，非若威之有所…
translation_en:
"It is virtue alone that moves Heaven; there is no distance to which it does not reach. Pride brings loss, and humility receives increase—this is the Way of Heaven." [Book of Documents, "Counsels of the Great Yu"]

Jiang Wenming 江文明

Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies (xuezheng) Huang comments: [The difficulty of this topic lies in connecting its parts; in the examination hall, other writers failed to make them correspond. In this essay, the principles and ideas are harmoniously integrated, and the phrasing is thoroughly nuanced—something impossible for anyone not profound in self-cultivation. It should be recorded as a model for the four quarters.]

Associate Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies (jiaoshou) Sun comments: [Lofty in insight and profound in principle, it thoroughly brings out the subtlety of the resonance between Heaven and humanity—not merely on account of its literary style alone. Deeply admirable, deeply admirable!]

Examiner and Right Companion of the Heir Apparent (you zhongyun) He comments: [Clear and fluent; a masterwork of the examination arts [?].]

Examiner and Left Companion of the Heir Apparent (zuo zhongyun) Fan comments: [The essay grasps the pivotal points; worth recording.]

The great minister speaks to the utmost of how virtue moves Heaven, and thereby elucidates it through the Way of Heaven. Now, the sympathetic resonance of virtue knows no barrier even at the remoteness of Heaven. Bringing loss to the proud and increase to the humble—even Heaven does not go against this, how much less so humanity! It was with these words that Boyi 伯益 assisted Yu 禹.

It is as if he said: Supreme virtue is the source of sympathetic response; waxing and waning are the principle of contraction and expansion. Since the Miao 苗 people have not yet submitted, in their foolishness [? or: "Yu 禹" misprinted as 蠢], should you not also turn back to look within yourself and seek the fundamental clue in Heaven? That those obstinate ones do not come to their tasks shows that awe cannot control them; that laboring the troops is of no avail shows that force cannot be relied upon.

Only one who makes his virtue shine to the utmost does not merely move men alone. Its fragrant aroma ascends and communicates with the august and profound; although the substance of Heaven is supremely distant, the manifest arrival of his spiritual essence cannot be confined by physical location—unlike awe, which has places it…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
至有所不至矣任德之純者非特動物已也精
華上達於貞觀雖天本廣遠而神化之感孚形
迹不能爲之間非若力之有所及有所不及矣
夫觀其所以動天者而人可知也不觀天之所
以爲天乎蓋天道不外乎陰陽而進退相乘于
不已自其進而得夫既生之數者謂之滿滿不
期損也而裒多之節若或招之上天虧盈之道
本如是也否則進者日進而氣化不幾于紊乎
自其退而得夫未生之數者謂之謙謙非求益
===
也而滋至之幾若或受之上天益謙之道本如
是也否則退者日退而造化不幾於息乎夫觀
德之動天則知感化有機而修德不可緩矣觀
天之福謙則知天人一理而滿假不可形矣吁
益之贊禹固以祇承于帝也然而罔愆之德舍
己之謙帝豈待贊而後有邪蓋聖不自聖帝德
之益隆也責難無已帝臣之交儆也卒之干羽
舞而有苗格則修德之言爲可驗而受謙之福
非虛語矣此來王率服之化萬世爲獨盛也哉
punctuated: 至，有所不至矣；任德之純者，非特動物已也，精華上達於貞觀，雖天本廣遠，而神化之感孚，形迹不能爲之間，非若力之有所及，有所不及矣。夫觀其所以動天者，而人可知也。不觀天之所以爲天乎？蓋天道不外乎陰陽，而進退相乘于不已。自其進而得夫既生之數者謂之滿，滿不期損也，而裒多之節若或招之，上天虧盈之道本如是也，否則進者日進，而氣化不幾于紊乎？自其退而得夫未生之數者謂之謙，謙非求益也，而滋至之幾若或受之，上天益謙之道本如是也，否則退者日退，而造化不幾於息乎？夫觀德之動天，則知感化有機，而修德不可緩矣；觀天之福謙，則知天人一理，而滿假不可形矣。吁！益之贊禹，固以祇承于帝也。然而罔愆之德、舍己之謙，帝豈待贊而後有邪？蓋聖不自聖，帝德之益隆也；責難無已，帝臣之交儆也。卒之干羽舞而有苗格，則修德之言爲可驗，而受謙之福非虛語矣。此來王率服之化，萬世爲獨盛也哉！
translation_en: … reaches and places it does not reach. As for one who relies on the purity of virtue, he does not merely move living creatures; its finest essence ascends to reach the constant manifestation above. Although Heaven is fundamentally vast and distant, the responsive trust of spiritual transformation cannot be obstructed by physical traces—unlike force, which has things it can reach and things it cannot reach. Now, by observing that whereby it moves Heaven, one may know how it affects men. And do we not observe that whereby Heaven is Heaven? Indeed, the Way of Heaven does not lie outside of yin and yang, whose advance and retreat alternate in endless succession. From the aspect of its advancing and attaining the numbers already brought into being, it is called fullness. Fullness does not expect diminution, yet the regulation that reduces excess seems as though invited by it; such is fundamentally the Way of High Heaven in diminishing the full—otherwise, what advances would advance day by day, and would the transformations of vital force not nearly fall into disorder? From the aspect of its retreating and holding to the numbers not yet brought into being, it is called humility. Humility does not seek increase, yet the subtle workings of growing abundance seem as though received by it; such is fundamentally the Way of High Heaven in increasing the humble—otherwise, what retreats would retreat day by day, and would the creative transformations of nature not nearly cease? Thus, when we observe how virtue moves Heaven, we know that moral transformation has its pivotal mechanism, and the cultivation of virtue cannot be delayed; when we observe how Heaven blesses the humble, we know that Heaven and man share a single principle, and arrogance and self-satisfaction must not be allowed to take form. Ah! Yi's counsel to Yu was assuredly meant so that he might reverently comply with the Sovereign [Shun]. Yet as for flawless virtue and the humility of setting aside one's own views, how could the Sovereign have waited upon such counsel before possessing them? Rather, being sage and yet not regarding himself as sage was how the Sovereign's virtue grew ever more exalted; urging difficult duties upon him without cease was how the Sovereign's ministers admonished one another. In the end, when shields and feathers were danced and the lord of Miao submitted, the words about cultivating virtue were proven true, and the blessing received by humility was no empty talk! Was not this transforming influence, whereby all came to acknowledge the king and led one another into submission, uniquely flourishing for ten thousand generations?

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
小大之臣咸懷忠良其侍御僕從罔匪正
人以旦夕承弼厥辟
蔡立身
同考試官學正黃　批〔整齊峻潔講侍御承弼處尤多雋永可以一洗浮冗之習矣〕
同考試官教授孫　批〔氣象優裕詞旨懇到〕
聖世得人之盛宛然可想
考試官右中允何　批〔明爽剴切深得題意〕
考試官左中允范　批〔詞旨精到〕
===
賢王舉先世得人之盛而猶多助于近臣焉夫
君德係于所養也得人如文武而猶賴近臣之
助況後世乎穆王之命伯冏若謂輔德以擇人
爲先正君以邇臣爲要聰明齊聖文武之德盛
矣使其德雖天縱而臣不皆賢猶曰有君而無
臣也惟時小大之臣列爵雖不同矣而篤棐之
心則同凡進思盡忠以助成王之德顯者不獨
小臣爲然而大者胥爲之倡也受任雖不一矣
而精白之忱則一凡願爲良臣以輔厥后之惟
punctuated:
小大之臣，咸懷忠良。其侍御僕從，罔匪正人，以旦夕承弼厥辟。
蔡立身
同考試官學正黃　批〔整齊峻潔，講侍御承弼處尤多雋永，可以一洗浮冗之習矣。〕
同考試官教授孫　批〔氣象優裕，詞旨懇到，聖世得人之盛，宛然可想。〕
考試官右中允何　批〔明爽剴切，深得題意。〕
考試官左中允范　批〔詞旨精到。〕

賢王舉先世得人之盛，而猶多助于近臣焉。夫君德係于所養也，得人如文、武，而猶賴近臣之助，況後世乎？穆王之命伯冏，若謂：輔德以擇人爲先，正君以邇臣爲要。聰明齊聖，文、武之德盛矣。使其德雖天縱，而臣不皆賢，猶曰有君而無臣也。惟時小大之臣，列爵雖不同矣，而篤棐之心則同，凡進思盡忠，以助成王之德顯者，不獨小臣爲然，而大者胥爲之倡也；受任雖不一矣，而精白之忱則一，凡願爲良臣，以輔厥后之惟
translation_en:
"The ministers, both small and great, all cherished loyalty and goodness. Their attendants, charioteers, and personal servants were none of them other than upright men, who morning and night supported and corrected their sovereign."

Cai Lishen 蔡立身

Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Instructor (xuezheng) Huang 黃 comments: [Well-ordered, lofty, and pure. The discussion of the attendants supporting and correcting the sovereign is especially rich and meaningful, enough to wash away the habit of superficiality and verbosity.]
Associate Examiner and Prefectural Instructor (jiaoshou) Sun 孫 comments: [Its spirit is composed and abundant, its words and purport earnest and thorough; the flourishing recruitment of worthy men in a sage age can be vividly imagined.]
Examiner and Right Companion to the Heir Apparent (you zhongyun) He 何 comments: [Clear, brisk, and incisive; it deeply grasps the meaning of the theme.]
Examiner and Left Companion to the Heir Apparent (zuo zhongyun) Fan 范 comments: [The diction and purport are refined and thorough.]

The worthy king cites the flourishing of men of talent obtained in former generations, yet still attributes much to the assistance of close attendants. Now, the ruler's virtue depends on how it is nourished. Even when obtaining men as Kings Wen 文 and Wu 武 did, they still relied on the aid of close attendants—how much more so in later generations! When King Mu 穆王 charged Bo Jiong 伯冏, it was as if to say: in assisting virtue, selecting the right men comes first; in rectifying the ruler, close attendants are essential. Intelligent, sagely, and wise, the virtue of Kings Wen and Wu was abundant indeed. Yet even though their virtue was heaven-bestowed, had their ministers not all been worthy, one would still say there was a ruler but no ministers. At that time, among the ministers small and great, although their ranks of nobility differed, their heart of笃実 (earnest) assistance was the same. In all cases of coming forward with thoughts of exhausting loyalty so as to help bring the illustriousness of the king's virtue to completion, it was not only the lesser ministers who did so, but the great ones all took the lead for them. Although the charges they received were not uniform, their pure and spotless sincerity was one. In all cases of wishing to be good ministers so as to assist their sovereign's…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
明者不特大臣爲然而小者罔不同心也夫臣
無分于小大而德悉秉乎忠良上下道同宜無
待于近習之助矣乃當時之爲侍御僕從者又
皆遴選于知恤之嚴而迪簡乎庶常之吉志慮
端方邪僻非所間也而以此朝夕乎王宮美則
承而違則弼蓋無時無處而非薰陶之所矣是
其心即濟濟多士之心也而其功不尤要哉言
行亮直便佞非所與也而以此出入乎禁闥順
其正而匡其邪蓋一動一息而皆漸染之機矣
===
是其選即藹藹吉人之選也而其助不愈密哉
吁此文武之德化所由益盛也穆王舉以告伯
冏其望之一何至邪抑考左右僕御古愼其選
故書敘綴衣虎賁與三事並詩錄膳夫趣馬爲
六卿屬而必擇正人以充之三代而上培養君
德恃有此具也自此意不明而儇敏是用故明
諍顯諫于大廷而潛滋默誘于深宮者往往是
矣後世欲致君爲文武者當三復于伯冏之篇
詩
punctuated:
明者，不特大臣爲然，而小者罔不同心也。夫臣無分于小大，而德悉秉乎忠良，上下道同，宜無待于近習之助矣。乃當時之爲侍御僕從者，又皆遴選于知恤之嚴，而迪簡乎庶常之吉。志慮端方，邪僻非所間也；而以此朝夕乎王宮，美則承而違則弼，蓋無時無處而非薰陶之所矣。是其心即濟濟多士之心也，而其功不尤要哉？言行亮直，便佞非所與也；而以此出入乎禁闥，順其正而匡其邪，蓋一動一息而皆漸染之機矣。是其選即藹藹吉人之選也，而其助不愈密哉？吁！此文、武之德化所由益盛也。穆王舉以告伯冏，其望之一何至邪！抑考左右僕御，古愼其選。故《書》敘綴衣、虎賁與三事並，《詩》錄膳夫、趣馬爲六卿屬，而必擇正人以充之。三代而上，培養君德，恃有此具也。自此意不明，而儇敏是用，故明諍顯諫于大廷，而潛滋默誘于深宮者，往往是矣。後世欲致君爲文、武者，當三復于《伯冏》之篇。
《詩》
translation_en:
… enlightened—this was true not only of the great ministers, for the lesser ones all shared the same mind without exception. Now, when ministers without distinction of lesser or great all held fast to loyalty and goodness in their virtue, and superior and inferior shared the same Way, there should have been no need to rely upon the assistance of close attendants. Yet those who served as personal attendants and grooms at that time were also all carefully selected through strict discernment and concern, and chosen from among the auspicious men of the regular positions. Their intentions and thoughts were upright and square, with no room for perversity or obliquity; and as such men attended the royal palace morning and evening, complying with what was admirable and correcting what was errant, there was truly no time and no place that was not a site of moral cultivation. Thus their minds were none other than the minds of the stately multitude of officers—and was not their achievement even more vital? Their words and deeds were honest and upright, having nothing to do with specious flattery; and as such men went in and out of the forbidden palace gates, following what was proper in the ruler and rectifying what was crooked, every movement and every breath was an opportunity for gradual salutary influence. Thus their selection was none other than the selection of the harmonious and auspicious men—and was not their assistance even more intimate?

Ah! This is how the virtuous transformation of King Wen and King Wu grew ever more flourishing. When King Mu cited this in his charge to Bo Jiong, how profound were his hopes for him! Moreover, if we examine the personal attendants and grooms of antiquity, their selection was treated with great caution. Thus the Book of Documents (Shu) lists the Keeper of the Robes and the Tiger Braves alongside the Three Affairs [the three top ministerial posts], and the Book of Odes (Shi) records the Provisioner and the Master of the Royal Stables together with the Six Ministers, and upright men were always chosen to fill these posts. From the Three Dynasties on back, the nurturing of the ruler's virtue relied upon this very provision. Once this principle ceased to be understood and glib, clever men came to be employed instead, it frequently happened that while open remonstrance and forthright admonition took place in the grand court, secret corruption and silent seduction went on within the deep palace. Those in later ages who wish to lead their ruler to become like King Wen and King Wu ought to read the chapter "Bo Jiong" [Charge to Jiong] over and over again.

Book of Odes (Shi)

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
有馮有翼有孝有德以引以翼豈弟君子
四方爲則顒顒卬卬如圭如璋令聞令
望豈弟君子四方爲綱
汪蕃立
同考試官教諭丘　批〔爲則爲綱處全本得〕
〔賢自輔上來題意最難貫徹獨此作得之〕
同考試官教諭蔣　批〔體格整飭而脉絡過〕
〔接處渾無痕迹此邃養之作〕
同考試官教授黃　批〔發告君用賢意忠愛〕
===
〔藹然〕
同考試官知縣帥　批〔約題有體命詞尤工〕
考試官右中允何　批〔溫厚含蓄〕
考試官左中允范　批〔純雅醞藉宜録以式〕
大臣告君有言德之輔而法天下者有言德之
成而統天下者甚矣君德有關於天下也然必
得所輔而後成則親賢之益何大哉昔召公納
誨于王旣因卷阿游詠之暇而歆以壽考福祿
之盛矣此乃言其所由致也若曰天下之屬望
punctuated:
「有馮有翼，有孝有德，以引以翼。豈弟君子，四方爲則。顒顒卬卬，如圭如璋，令聞令望。豈弟君子，四方爲綱。」
汪蕃立
同考試官教諭丘　批：〔爲則爲綱處，全本得賢自輔上來。題意最難貫徹，獨此作得之。〕
同考試官教諭蔣　批：〔體格整飭，而脉絡過接處渾無痕迹，此邃養之作。〕
同考試官教授黃　批：〔發告君用賢意，忠愛藹然。〕
同考試官知縣帥　批：〔約題有體，命詞尤工。〕
考試官右中允何　批：〔溫厚含蓄。〕
考試官左中允范　批：〔純雅醞藉，宜録以式。〕
大臣告君，有言德之輔而法天下者，有言德之成而統天下者。甚矣，君德有關於天下也！然必得所輔而後成，則親賢之益何大哉！昔召公納誨于王，旣因卷阿游詠之暇，而歆以壽考福祿之盛矣，此乃言其所由致也。若曰：天下之屬望
translation_en:
"You have helpers and supporters, men of filial piety and virtue, to lead and to assist you. Easy and self-possessed sovereign, the four quarters take you as their pattern. Dignified and majestic, like a jade scepter, like a half-scepter, of令good renown and high reputation. Easy and self-possessed sovereign, the four quarters take you as their regulator."

Wang Fanli 汪蕃立

Associate Examiner and Instructor Qiu 丘 comments: 〔The points about "being a pattern" and "being a regulator" are entirely rooted in obtaining worthy men to assist oneself. The meaning of the topic is most difficult to carry through coherently, yet this composition alone achieves it.〕
Associate Examiner and Instructor Jiang 蔣 comments: 〔The structure and form are orderly and disciplined, while the transitions connecting the veins of thought leave no trace at all; this is a work of profound cultivation.〕
Associate Examiner and Professor Huang 黃 comments: 〔It brings out the meaning of advising the sovereign to employ the worthy, brimming with loyal affection.〕
Associate Examiner and District Magistrate Shuai 帥 comments: 〔It summarizes the topic with proper form, and its phrasing is especially skillful.〕
Examiner and Right Companion He 何 comments: 〔Gentle, generous, and restrained.〕
Examiner and Left Companion Fan 范 comments: 〔Pure, elegant, and poised; it should be recorded as a model.〕

When a great minister counsels his sovereign, he speaks first of how his virtue is assisted so as to serve as a model for the world, and then of how his virtue is brought to completion so as to govern the world. Profound indeed is the bearing of the sovereign's virtue upon the world! Yet it is only after obtaining those who assist him that his virtue is brought to completion—how great, then, is the benefit of drawing near to the worthy! In antiquity, when the Duke of Shao (Shao Gong 召公) offered instruction to the King, having taken the occasion of their leisure in roaming and singing at the curving slope (Juan'e 卷阿) to inspire him with the abundance of longevity, good fortune, and blessings, in these lines he spoke of how such things are brought about. It is as if he said: The expectations of the world…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
在君德君德之成就在賢才今也師表王國多
老成端亮之倫而爲馮爲翼者有之布列王朝
皆慈祥篤實之選而爲孝爲德者有之誠以引
馬以翼馬或疑承于後先或弼輔于左右夫德
之有輔如此將見涵養深而居與之化言惟作
令也趨嚮正而習與之成動惟作式也豈弟君
子四方不爲則乎何也君者民所則而馮翼孝
德之助固君德之所由成也是故語德範則大
觀在上而顒卬昭度何尊嚴也語德器則清明
===
在躬而圭璋比質何純潔也且令聞馬令望馬
德音起明明之頌德容示穆穆之光夫德之有
成如此將見修身以建其極而慕德者悉入於
範圍罔不承令矣恭已以握其樞而仰德者咸
歸於怙冐罔不承式矣豈弟君子四方不爲綱
乎何也君者民之綱而顒卬圭璋之德固民心
之所由屬也夫如是則人與之天與之而壽考
福祿亦在其中矣王誠有意于斯則任賢修德
可不是務乎抑觀戴記保傅篇其言四輔之設
punctuated: 在君德，君德之成就在賢才。今也師表王國，多老成端亮之倫，而「爲馮爲翼」者有之；布列王朝，皆慈祥篤實之選，而「爲孝爲德」者有之。誠「以引」馬、「以翼」馬，或疑承于後先，或弼輔于左右。夫德之有輔如此，將見涵養深而居與之化，言惟作令也；趨嚮正而習與之成，動惟作式也。「豈弟君子」，「四方」不「爲則」乎？何也？君者，民所則，而馮翼、孝德之助，固君德之所由成也。是故語德範，則大觀在上，而「顒卬」昭度，何尊嚴也！語德器，則清明在躬，而「圭璋」比質，何純潔也！且「令聞」馬、「令望」馬，德音起明明之頌，德容示穆穆之光。夫德之有成如此，將見修身以建其極，而慕德者悉入於範圍，罔不承令矣；恭已以握其樞，而仰德者咸歸於怙冐，罔不承式矣。「豈弟君子」，「四方」不「爲綱」乎？何也？君者，民之綱，而顒卬、圭璋之德，固民心之所由屬也。夫如是，則人與之，天與之，而壽考福祿亦在其中矣。王誠有意于斯，則任賢修德，可不是務乎？抑觀《戴記·保傅篇》，其言四輔之設…
translation_en: …rests on the sovereign's virtue, and the perfection of the sovereign's virtue rests on worthy men of talent. Now, standing as models for the royal state, there are many men of mature judgment and upright integrity, so that there are those who "can be leaned upon and can give support"; arrayed in the royal court, all are chosen for their benevolence and sincere solidity, so that there are those who "possess filial piety and possess virtue." Truly, "to lead" the king on [reading 馬 as 焉] and "to assist" him [reading 馬 as 焉], some resolve his doubts and attend him before and behind, while others counsel and aid him on his left and right. When his virtue has such assistance as this, we shall see that his moral cultivation becomes deep and his daily life transforms along with them, so that his words become ordinances; his orientation becomes upright and his habits are formed along with them, so that his actions become models. "Easy and self-possessed is our prince"—will not "the four quarters" take him "as their pattern"? Why is this? The ruler is he whom the people take as their pattern, and the aid of those who can be leaned upon, give support, and possess filial piety and virtue is indeed the means by which the ruler's virtue is brought to completion. Therefore, if we speak of his moral demeanor, he is a grand spectacle on high, and as he manifests his standard in a manner "majestic and revered," how august he is! If we speak of his moral capacity, clear brightness resides within his person, and as his substance is compared to "a jade tablet or half-tablet," how pure and spotless he is! Moreover, he has "aContinuously good reputation" [reading 馬 as 焉] and "a goodly outlook" [reading 馬 as 焉]; his virtuous voice gives rise to praises of his resplendent brightness, and his virtuous countenance displays a solemn and reverent light. When his virtue is perfected like this, we shall see that he cultivates his person to establish the supreme standard, and those who yearn for his virtue all enter within his compass, none failing to obey his ordinances; he holds himself in reverent composure to grasp the pivot of governance, and those who look up to his virtue all turn to his sheltering protection, none failing to follow his model. "Easy and self-possessed is our prince"—will he not "be the guiding cord" of "the four quarters"? Why is this? The ruler is the guiding cord of the people, and his majestic, revered, and jade-like virtue is indeed that to which the hearts of the people attach themselves. When it is like this, then men will side with him and Heaven will side with him, and longevity, felicity, and official emolument will also be found therein. If the King truly sets his mind upon this, then can he fail to make employing the worthy and cultivating virtue his urgent task? Yet if we examine the chapter "The Protectors and Tutors" (Baofu pian) in the Record of Ritual by Dai (Daiji), its account of the establishment of the Four Assistants…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
詳矣而召公猶惓惓焉豈不以君子易踈小人
易親其成也衆君子輔之而不足其敗也一小
人雜之而有餘故此詩歷數馮翼孝德而要其
成於豈弟以見任賢專而養德純人臣之所以
格君心者固無用才敏辯給爲也愼簡引翼之
士宜於此察之
於乎皇考永世克孝念茲皇祖陟降庭止
蔡惟亨
同考試官教諭丘　批〔成王追慕之意發之〕
〔真切而體貼孝永陟降等語尤覺明透〕
===
同考試官教諭蔣　批〔聖孝純切處最難形〕
〔容此獨發揮懇至非凡作者〕
同考試官教授黃　批〔聖孝永言之思模寫〕
〔殆盡〕
同考試官知縣帥　批〔咏嘆得體精於詩者〕
考試官右中允何　批〔形容念祖處宛然〕
考試官左中允范　批〔簡潔精邃〕
嘆先王之純乎孝以先王之心乎親夫作求世
punctuated:
詳矣，而召公猶惓惓焉，豈不以君子易踈、小人易親？其成也，衆君子輔之而不足；其敗也，一小人雜之而有餘。故此詩歷數馮翼孝德，而要其成於豈弟，以見任賢專而養德純。人臣之所以格君心者，固無用才敏辯給爲也。愼簡引翼之士，宜於此察之。

於乎皇考，永世克孝，念茲皇祖，陟降庭止。
蔡惟亨
同考試官教諭丘　批〔成王追慕之意，發之真切，而體貼孝永、陟降等語，尤覺明透。〕
同考試官教諭蔣　批〔聖孝純切處最難形容，此獨發揮懇至，非凡作者。〕
同考試官教授黃　批〔聖孝永言之思，模寫殆盡。〕
同考試官知縣帥　批〔咏嘆得體，精於詩者。〕
考試官右中允何　批〔形容念祖處宛然。〕
考試官左中允范　批〔簡潔精邃。〕

嘆先王之純乎孝，以先王之心乎親。夫作求世
translation_en:
… is explained in detail, and yet the Duke of Shao (Shao gong 召公) remained so earnestly concerned—was this not because gentlemen of virtue are easily estranged while petty men are easily drawn close? In bringing virtue to completion, even a multitude of gentlemen assisting the ruler is not enough; in ruining it, a single petty man mixed in among them is more than enough. Therefore, this ode enumerates in turn "those you can lean on and those who give you wings, those of filial piety and those of virtue," and sums up their perfection in the "joyous and pleasant lord," so as to show that when the employment of worthies is exclusive, the cultivation of virtue becomes pure. That whereby a minister rectifies his ruler's mind certainly has no use for cleverness of talent or glibness of speech. Those who carefully select men to guide and support the sovereign ought to examine the matter here.

"Oh, my august deceased father! / Throughout all his life he was able to be filial. / Thinking of this august grandfather of mine, / Who ascended and descended in the court."
Cai Weiheng 蔡惟亨
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Qiu 丘 comments: 〔King Cheng's (Cheng wang 成王) sentiment of cherishing the memory of his predecessors is brought out with genuine earnestness, and the close attention paid to expressions such as "perpetually filial" and "ascending and descending" feels especially clear and penetrating.〕
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Jiang 蔣 comments: 〔Where the sage's filial piety is purest and most earnest is the hardest thing to describe; this essay alone expounds it with sincere thoroughness—no ordinary writer.〕
Associate Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Huang 黃 comments: 〔The sage's enduring thoughts of filial devotion are depicted almost to perfection.〕
Associate Examiner and District Magistrate Shuai 帥 comments: 〔The chanting and exclamation hit the proper tone; one who has mastered the Book of Odes (Shi 詩).〕
Examiner and Right Companion to the Heir Apparent He 何 comments: 〔It depicts his mindfulness of his grandfather vividly, as if before one's eyes.〕
Examiner and Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Fan 范 comments: 〔Concise, clean, refined, and profound.〕

He sighs in admiration at how the former king was pure in his filial piety, because the former king's heart was devoted to his parent. Now, to actively seek out the hereditary…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
德天子之孝也故知先王思親之心則知其所
以爲孝矣此成王始朝于廟而歌之也謂夫予
今纘皇考之緒固當率皇考之道於乎我皇考
也大烈丕承既昭嗣服之休大孝不匱復篤終
身之慕配鎬京而禋清廟人知其爲孝矣然非
一時之孝乃永世之孝也成王孚而式下土人
知其孝之永矣然非徒孝之文乃克孝之實也
何以言之蓋皇考克念厥紹恒沒世而不忘故
皇祖於昭于天雖異世而如見思其所志則精
===
誠之極與之相流通一陟一降若或履其位焉
宛乎亹亹穆穆之儀刑也而所以善繼之者豈
敢忽乎思其所事則著存之感與之相對越當
宁當扆若或臨其庭焉恍乎肅肅雝雝之軌度
也而所以善述之者豈敢遺乎是蓋目所常接
固可見其孝心之誠而心所常存又可見其孝
思之永然則今日之念皇考亦猶當時之念皇
祖也紹庭上下予何敢忘皇考之孝哉嗟乎自
古國家肇造鴻業其祖考身歷艱難意慮深遠
punctuated: 德，天子之孝也。故知先王思親之心，則知其所以爲孝矣。此成王始朝于廟而歌之也。謂夫予今纘皇考之緒，固當率皇考之道。於乎我皇考也！大烈丕承，既昭嗣服之休；大孝不匱，復篤終身之慕。配鎬京而禋清廟，人知其爲孝矣，然非一時之孝，乃永世之孝也；成王孚而式下土，人知其孝之永矣，然非徒孝之文，乃克孝之實也。何以言之？蓋皇考克念厥紹，恒沒世而不忘，故皇祖於昭于天，雖異世而如見。思其所志，則精誠之極與之相流通，一陟一降，若或履其位焉，宛乎亹亹穆穆之儀刑也，而所以善繼之者，豈敢忽乎？思其所事，則著存之感與之相對越，當宁當扆，若或臨其庭焉，恍乎肅肅雝雝之軌度也，而所以善述之者，豈敢遺乎？是蓋目所常接，固可見其孝心之誠；而心所常存，又可見其孝思之永。然則今日之念皇考，亦猶當時之念皇祖也。紹庭上下，予何敢忘皇考之孝哉！嗟乎！自古國家肇造鴻業，其祖考身歷艱難，意慮深遠，
translation_en: …virtue is the filial piety of the Son of Heaven. Therefore, if one understands the former king's heart in longing for his parent, one understands that whereby he was filial. This was sung by King Cheng when he first held court in the ancestral temple. He said: Now that I continue the line of my August Deceased Father [King Wu], I ought assuredly to follow the Way of my August Deceased Father. Oh, my August Deceased Father! Grandly receiving the great meritorious work, he already made bright the excellence of succeeding to the charge; his great filial piety being unfailing, he furthermore deepened his lifelong yearning. Matching him with heaven at the capital of Hao and offering pure sacrifice in the Pure Temple—people knew that this was filial piety; yet it was not the filial piety of a single moment, but the filial piety of perpetual generations. Completing the kingly trust and serving as a model to the lower earth—people knew that his filial piety was perpetual; yet it was not merely the outward form of filial piety, but the substance of being truly filial. How do we say this? Because my August Deceased Father was able to be mindful of his succession, constantly never forgetting until the end of his life; therefore our August Ancestor [King Wen] shines brightly in Heaven, and though of a different age, it was as if he were seen in person. When he thought of what he aimed at, the utmost of his pure sincerity circulated and communicated with him—ascending and descending, it was as if he were treading his very position, vividly displaying his tireless and profound model of deportment! And in the means of skilfully continuing his will, how could he dare be neglectful? When he thought of what he undertook, the sense of his manifest presence responded to him face to face—standing between door and screen or before the ceremonial axe-screen, it was as if he were presiding over his very court, vividly revealing his reverent and harmonious standard and measure! And in the means of skilfully carrying forward his affairs, how could he dare omit anything? Thus, from what his eyes constantly encountered, one may indeed see the sincerity of his filial heart; and from what his mind constantly preserved, one may further see the perpetuity of his filial thoughts. This being so, my mindfulness of my August Deceased Father today is just like his mindfulness of our August Ancestor in those days. Continuing the succession as he ascends and descends in the court, how could I dare forget the filial piety of my August Deceased Father! Alas! Since antiquity, when a state first founds a great enterprise, its ancestors and fathers personally pass through hardships and difficulties, and their thoughts and plans are deep and far-reaching; …

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
定典法以貽後人乃其子孫弗念或狹小其制
度而紛更之國家遂以多事故周公陳戒曰無
忝爾祖而成王於朝廟亦首言之不獨承考之
孝蓋兢兢然有法祖之思焉嗚呼此所以能保
文武成業而垂休無疆也
春秋
春王正月城楚丘〔僖公二年〕夏叔詣會晉
趙鞅宋樂大心衛北宮喜鄭游吉曹人
邾人滕人薛人小邾人于黃父〔昭公二〕
十有五年
===
錢達道
同考試官推官劉　批〔發聖人以正待人意〕
〔最爲明透且融貫左史飾以新詞眞文之佳者〕
錄之
考試官右中允何　批〔善發傳意〕
考試官左中允范　批〔詞整意足錄之〕
春秋以正待人于封國勤王之功而皆無美焉
此楚丘之城則專大權黃父之會則修常職也
punctuated:
定典法以貽後人。乃其子孫弗念，或狹小其制度而紛更之，國家遂以多事。故周公陳戒曰：「無忝爾祖。」而成王於朝廟亦首言之，不獨承考之孝，蓋兢兢然有法祖之思焉。嗚呼！此所以能保文、武成業，而垂休無疆也。

《春秋》：「春，王正月，城楚丘。」〔僖公二年〕「夏，叔詣會晉趙鞅、宋樂大心、衛北宮喜、鄭游吉、曹人、邾人、滕人、薛人、小邾人于黃父。」〔昭公二〕十有五年

錢達道
同考試官推官劉　批：〔發聖人以正待人意，〕〔最爲明透。且融貫左史，飾以新詞，眞文之佳者。〕錄之。
考試官右中允何　批：〔善發傳意。〕
考試官左中允范　批：〔詞整意足，錄之。〕

《春秋》以正待人，于封國、勤王之功，而皆無美焉。此楚丘之城則專大權，黃父之會則修常職也。
translation_en:
…established institutional laws to bequeath to their descendants. Yet when their descendants fail to keep them in mind, or consider their institutions too narrow and small and rashly alter them, the state consequently falls into turmoil. Therefore, when the Duke of Zhou presented his admonition, he said, "Do not disgrace your ancestors." And King Cheng, in holding court in the ancestral temple, also spoke of this first of all; he did not merely carry on the filial piety of his late father, but was cautiously and reverently mindful of emulating his grandfather. Alas! This is how he was able to preserve the accomplished enterprise of Kings Wen and Wu, and hand down blessings without limit.

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"In spring, in the King's first month, they walled Chuqiu." [Second year of Duke Xi] "In summer, Shu Yi met with Zhao Yang of Jin, Yue Daxin of Song, Beigong Xi of Wei, You Ji of Zheng, a man of Cao, a man of Zhu, a man of Teng, a man of Xue, and a man of Little Zhu at Huangfu." [Twenty]-fifth year [of Duke Zhao]

Qian Dadao 錢達道
Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Liu 劉 comments: [It brings out the Sage's intention of holding people to correctness with the greatest clarity and penetration. Moreover, it thoroughly integrates the Zuo History (Zuo zhuan) and adorns it with fresh phrasing—truly a fine piece of writing.] Record it.
Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent He 何 comments: [Skillfully brings out the meaning of the Commentary.]
Examiner, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Fan 范 comments: [The phrasing is well-ordered and the meaning complete; record it.]

The Spring and Autumn Annals holds people to correctness; thus, with regard to the achievements of enfeoffing a state and rallying to the King's service, in neither case does it offer praise. For the walling of Chuqiu was a usurpation of great authority, while the meeting at Huangfu was merely the performance of regular duty. …

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
宜經均無美歟楚丘曷城也渡河廬野而許人
有載馳之賦衛國已亡矣桓也遷其地以封之
是得興滅之仁者而經顧無美詞何蓋衛祀可
封也自伯者而封之則權其專矣獨不聞設轍
扆作策命乃天子馭貴之典乎今也惠將徼于
康叔命不請于周王戍以甲士馬歸其祭服焉
無虧一遣而衛以忘亡功則誠大矣然憫人之
亡而再造焉是敢建諸侯也而可以訓乎噫木
瓜之頌固德齊之深也彼竊作福之權而樹恩
===
攘善奚足道之故經于楚丘而深沒其迹以此
黃父曷會也攻瑕及杏而大叔懷鉼罄之羞王
室則蠢矣須也申其會以謀之是得尊王之義
者而經亦無美詞何蓋王事宜勤也以諸侯而
勤之則職之常矣獨不聞彤弓一彤矢百有天
王扞艱之寄乎今也憂方感于鄭臣會即徵于
列國輸其王粟具以戍人馬簡子一言而衆
無異議事則已勤矣然急君之難而宣力焉殆
非異人任也而敢謂勞乎噫嫠婦之微尚憂周
punctuated:
宜經均無美歟？楚丘曷城也？渡河廬野，而許人有《載馳》之賦，衛國已亡矣。桓也遷其地以封之，是得興滅之仁者，而經顧無美詞，何？蓋衛祀可封也，自伯者而封之，則權其專矣。獨不聞設轍扆、作策命，乃天子馭貴之典乎？今也惠將徼于康叔，命不請于周王；戍以甲士馬，歸其祭服焉。無虧一遣，而衛以忘亡，功則誠大矣。然憫人之亡而再造焉，是敢建諸侯也，而可以訓乎？噫！《木瓜》之頌，固德齊之深也；彼竊作福之權，而樹恩攘善，奚足道之？故經于楚丘而深沒其迹，以此。

黃父曷會也？攻瑕及杏，而大叔懷鉼罄之羞，王室則蠢矣。須也申其會以謀之，是得尊王之義者，而經亦無美詞，何？蓋王事宜勤也，以諸侯而勤之，則職之常矣。獨不聞彤弓一、彤矢百，有天王扞艱之寄乎？今也憂方感于鄭臣，會即徵于列國；輸其王粟，具以戍人馬。簡子一言，而衆無異議，事則已勤矣。然急君之難而宣力焉，殆非異人任也，而敢謂勞乎？噫！嫠婦之微，尚憂周…
translation_en:
…Is it not fitting that the Classic gives praise to neither of them?

Why was Chuqiu walled? Having crossed the Yellow River to camp in the wilds, while the wife of the ruler of Xu composed the ode "Zaichi" ("Galloping"), the state of Wei had already perished. Duke Huan of Qi relocated its site and enfeoffed it. In doing so, he achieved the benevolence of reviving an extinguished state; yet why does the Classic offer no words of praise? Because while the sacrifices of Wei ought to have been re-enfeoffed, for a hegemon to enfeoff them on his own initiative was to usurp authority. Have we not heard that setting up the screen embroidered with axes and issuing the bamboo-slip charge of investiture are the statutory prerogatives by which the Son of Heaven governs the noble? Now, seeking to win favor with the spirit of Kangshu, he did not request a mandate from the King of Zhou, yet garrisoned the place with armored soldiers and horses [?] and restored their sacrificial vestments. With a single dispatch of Prince Wukui, Wei was made to forget its ruin—the achievement was truly great! Yet to take pity on another's destruction and reconstitute his state is to presume to establish feudal lords. Can this be held up as a model? Alas! The eulogy in the ode "Mugua" ("Quince") indeed reflects deep gratitude toward Qi; yet since he stole the prerogative of bestowing blessings in order to cultivate personal favor and appropriate goodness for himself, how is that worth commending? Therefore, in recording Chuqiu, the Classic deeply effaces the traces of his deed for this reason.

Why was the meeting at Huangfu held? When Xia and Xing were attacked, and Zitaishu of Zheng harbored the shame of "the pitcher being empty of disgrace to the jar," the royal house was in turmoil. Duke Qing of Jin [Xu] convened this meeting to take counsel for it. In doing so, he fulfilled the righteous duty of honoring the King; yet why does the Classic likewise offer no words of praise? Because the King's affairs ought to be diligently served, and for the feudal lords to labor in the King's service is simply their regular duty. Have we not heard that the gift of one red bow and a hundred red arrows carries the Heavenly King's commission to ward off distress? Now, no sooner was anxiety stirred by the minister of Zheng than a meeting was summoned among the various states to transport grain for the King and furnish garrison troops [?]. At a single word from Zhao Jianzi, the multitude raised no dissenting议 (opinion)—the service was diligent indeed! Yet to hasten to the ruler's crisis and exert one's strength is hardly a responsibility to be left to others; how then could one dare to claim it as a special merit? Alas! Even a humble widow still worries over the Zhou…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之闕也茍守維藩之職而棄義懷安將焉用之
故經于黃父而獨免于貶以此吁此春秋以正
待人之體也然甞諦觀之春秋之世烏可無桓
耶楚丘郎專已召伯一命投袂興師其匡王何
急也比朝之亂且數敗王師晉弗之省而今始
諰諰于一會何爲也哉頃也闇弱無桓之明范
獻諸臣非仲匹耳宜其不復振歟故爲國惟修
身之要而圖治以用賢爲先
冬十月甲午叔孫得臣敗狄于鹹〔文公十〕
有一年
===
顧起淹
同考試官推官劉　批〔春秋正名全爲修攘〕
punctuated:
之闕也，茍守維藩之職，而棄義懷安，將焉用之？故經于黃父而獨免于貶，以此。吁！此《春秋》以正待人之體也。然甞諦觀之，春秋之世，烏可無桓耶？楚丘、郎專已，召伯一命，投袂興師，其匡王何急也！比朝之亂，且數敗王師，晉弗之省，而今始諰諰于一會，何爲也哉？頃也闇弱，無桓之明；范獻諸臣，非仲匹耳。宜其不復振歟！故爲國惟修身之要，而圖治以用賢爲先。

冬，十月，甲午，叔孫得臣敗狄于鹹。〔文公十〕有一年。

顧起淹。
同考試官推官劉　批〔春秋正名，全爲修攘……〕
translation_en:
… [worry about the ruin] of Zhou; if those who hold the office of serving as a protective screen cast aside righteousness and cherish their own comfort, of what use will they be? Therefore, that the Classic at Huangfu alone spares them from censure is for this reason. Alas! This is the way the Spring and Autumn Annals treats men according to standard rectitude. Yet if we examine it closely, how could the world of the Spring and Autumn period do without Duke Huan [of Qi]? Though acts at Chuqiu and Lang were already taken on his own authority, as soon as the Earl of Shao brought the royal command, he flung down his sleeves and raised an army—how urgent he was in succoring the King! In the rebellion of Prince Chao, the royal armies were repeatedly defeated, yet Jin took no notice of it; and now it only begins to show anxious concern in a single covenant meeting—why is this? Duke Qing of Jin was benighted and weak, lacking the明 (discernment) of Duke Huan, while Fan Xianzi and the other ministers were simply no match for Guan Zhong. Is it any wonder that Jin could not revive its hegemony! Therefore, in governing a state, cultivating the ruler's own person is essential, and in planning for order, employing the worthy comes first.

"In winter, in the tenth month, on the day jiawu, Shusun Dechen defeated the Di at Xian." 〔Eleventh〕 year of Duke Wen.

Gu Qiyan 顧起淹.
Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Liu 劉, comments: 〔The rectification of names in the Spring and Autumn Annals is entirely for the purpose of internal cultivation and repelling external barbarians…〕

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之旨乎昔文之世狄敢侵伐齊又伐魯得臣前
而敗諸鹹傳曰敗者長狄僑如矣而經獨曰狄
于此而深感于聖人之意焉夫自畫疆以明限
也而夷之防以嚴怙强以亂華其窺伺之常也
自類族以別生也而夷之種以辨考系以審情
則制禦之本也此殷憂之在中國者而胡可忝
之玆得臣之所敗何狄也職方所圖非漆姓之
奸乎系牒所載非防風之裔乎今以遡稽
諸古也皆稱狄而未名爲長也雖喉以戈揰屍
===
維畝計特所獲者偶然耳可遂名其國耶於乎
入春秋狄之名或曰白或曰赤矣今之狄乃其
佚宕以内侵者也其强且寖長乎而烏可以忽
之乃其瓦石不能害者也一敗肯竟已乎而寧
弗爲慮之故特正其名焉曰斯所敗者狄也後
之人因其名而得以考焉考之而習險易之形
明强弱之勢其來也將利禦于門庭其不來也
則豫徹乎桑土此聖人之意也若不別而書後
將何考患之生無日矣抑是豈聖人有慨于時
punctuated: 之旨乎？昔文之世，狄敢侵伐齊，又伐魯。得臣前而敗諸鹹。《傳》曰：「敗者，長狄僑如矣。」而《經》獨曰「狄」，于此而深感于聖人之意焉。夫自畫疆以明限也，而夷之防以嚴；怙强以亂華，其窺伺之常也。自類族以別生也，而夷之種以辨；考系以審情，則制禦之本也。此殷憂之在中國者，而胡可忝之？玆得臣之所敗，何狄也？職方所圖，非漆姓之奸乎？系牒所載，非防風之裔乎？今以遡稽諸古也，皆稱狄，而未名爲長也。雖喉以戈揰，屍維畝計，特所獲者偶然耳，可遂名其國耶？於乎！入《春秋》，狄之名或曰「白」，或曰「赤」矣。今之狄，乃其佚宕以内侵者也，其强且寖長乎，而烏可以忽之？乃其瓦石不能害者也，一敗肯竟已乎，而寧弗爲慮之？故特正其名焉，曰：斯所敗者，狄也。後之人因其名而得以考焉，考之而習險易之形，明强弱之勢。其來也，將利禦于門庭；其不來也，則豫徹乎桑土。此聖人之意也。若不別而書，後將何考？患之生無日矣。抑是豈聖人有慨于時
translation_en: …principle of [rectifying names for the sake of internal cultivation and repelling outsiders]? In the past, during the reign of Duke Wen, the Di dared to invade and attack Qi, and also attacked Lu. [Shusun] Dechen advanced and defeated them at Xian. The Commentary says that the one defeated was Qiaoru of the Giant Di (Chang Di), yet the Classic alone simply calls them "Di." From this, one is deeply moved by the intention of the Sage. Now, ever since borders were drawn to clarify boundaries, the defense against the Yi barbarians has been made strict; relying on their strength to throw the Central States (Hua) into disorder is their constant habit of spying for opportunities. Ever since clans were categorized to distinguish lineages, the tribes of the Yi barbarians have been differentiated; examining their genealogies to ascertain their true conditions is the foundation of controlling and defending against them. This is a profound concern that rests with the Central States—how could one disgrace it [by confusion]? Now, what sort of Di were those defeated by Dechen? As mapped by the职方 (Director of Regions), were they not the villains of the Qi surname? As recorded in the genealogical registers, were they not the descendants of Fangfeng? Now, if we trace and examine them in antiquity, they were all called Di, and were never named "Giant" (Chang). Even though his throat was stabbed with a dagger-axe and his corpse measured by the mu, the one captured was merely an exceptional individual—how could one thereupon use that to name their state? Alas! Entering the Spring and Autumn period, the names of the Di were sometimes called "White" (Bai) and sometimes "Red" (Chi). The Di of this occasion were those who in their unbridled license invaded inward; their strength was gradually growing—how could one treat them with negligence? Moreover, they were those whom tiles and stones could not harm; after a single defeat, would they be willing to stop completely, and how could one not take precautions against them? Therefore, [the Sage] specially rectified their name, as if to say: Those who were defeated here were the Di. People of later generations, by relying on this name, are able to investigate them; by investigating them, they familiarize themselves with the terrain's difficulties and advantages, and clarify the relative dynamics of strength and weakness. When they come, one will advantageously defend against them at the courtyard gate; when they do not come, one will take advance precautions like gathering mulberry root-bark [to bind the nest]. This was the intention of the Sage. If they were recorded without proper distinction, what would later generations have to examine? Disasters would arise before long! Or did the Sage perhaps record this out of a lament for the times…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而書之耶狄自箕之役且四年畏縮而不敢動
豈非以晉襄故哉使能修攘斥之業以安中華
庶幾哉光嗣伯之烈乃坐緩事機而區區與秦
搆末矣靈也冲闇復何能爲則其敢于侵伐大
國而無忌憚也晉則啓之耳公羊謂大魯之敗
烏能掩晉之罪歟
禮記
王者功成作樂治定制禮其功大者其樂
備其治辯者其禮具
===
同考試官知縣徐　批〔詞意精新純雅粹然〕
天成非究心制作之原者不能作
考試官右中允何　批〔詞理精到〕
考試官左中允范　批〔思精詞雅一洗浮華可式〕
知聖王制作之原則知其所由盛矣蓋禮樂原
于治功也然非功大而治辯其可以言盛哉且
夫王者以聖人而在天子之位先天下而操制
作之權故樂以和民之聲非徒作也蓋聖王中
banxin: 鄉試錄文　四十八　袁應陽
punctuated:
而書之耶？狄自箕之役且四年，畏縮而不敢動，豈非以晉襄故哉？使能修攘斥之業以安中華，庶幾哉光嗣伯之烈；乃坐緩事機，而區區與秦搆，末矣。靈也冲闇，復何能爲？則其敢于侵伐大國而無忌憚也，晉則啓之耳。公羊謂大魯之敗，烏能掩晉之罪歟？
《禮記》
「王者功成作樂，治定制禮。其功大者其樂備，其治辯者其禮具。」
同考試官知縣徐　批〔詞意精新，純雅粹然，天成，非究心制作之原者不能作。〕
考試官右中允何　批〔詞理精到。〕
考試官左中允范　批〔思精詞雅，一洗浮華，可式。〕
知聖王制作之原，則知其所由盛矣。蓋禮樂原于治功也，然非功大而治辯，其可以言盛哉？且夫王者以聖人而在天子之位，先天下而操制作之權。故樂以和民之聲，非徒作也；蓋聖王中
translation_en:
… that he recorded it? Since the campaign at Ji, the Di had cowered and dared not stir for nearly four years—was this not because of Duke Xiang of Jin? Had he been able to cultivate the enterprise of repelling them so as to pacify the Central States, how close he would have come to glorifying his inherited hegemonic achievements! Instead, he sat idle and let opportunities slip away, engaging in petty feuds with Qin—how trivial! And since Duke Ling was young and benighted, what more could he accomplish? Thus, that the Di dared to invade and attack a great state without scruple was something that Jin itself invited. When the Gongyang Commentary says that it magnifies Lu's defeat of them, how could that cover up Jin's guilt?

Record of Rites (Liji):
"When a true king has accomplished his achievements, he composes music; when his governance is settled, he institutes rites. The greater his achievements, the more complete his music; the more comprehensive his governance, the more fully provisioned his rites."

Associate Examiner, District Magistrate Xu comments: [The diction and ideas are refined and fresh, purely elegant and unadorned, as if formed by nature; none who had not deeply investigated the origins of creating and instituting could have written this.]
Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent He comments: [The diction and reasoning are thorough and precise.]
Examiner, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Fan comments: [Thoughtful and refined, with elegant diction that washes away all superficiality; worthy as a model.]

When one understands the origin of the sage kings' creating and instituting, one understands whereby they flourished. For rites and music originate in governance and achievement; yet unless achievements are great and governance is comprehensive, how can one speak of their flourishing? Moreover, when a true king, being a sage, occupies the position of Son of Heaven, he leads the world and holds the authority to institute and create. Therefore, music serves to harmonize the voices of the people, and is not composed in vain; for when a sage king…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
天而興其建之爲功業者有凝成之美矣于是
乎立樂以昭吾之功于不窮雖文采節奏錯然
異變也孰非光烈之揄揚者乎禮以節民之心
非强制也蓋聖王嚮明而治其敷之爲化理者
有底定之休矣于是乎立禮以維吾之治于有
常雖制度文爲燦然異宜也孰非經綸之顯設
者乎由是觀之樂者功之象也功有未大樂難
乎備矣必也宏動之掀揭者巍巍乎冠百代而
獨隆夫然後九叙歌焉九成舞焉情文具舉美
===
善該矣金王相宣條理貫矣蓋所以感天地和
神人者在是而廣業崇功之氣象可挹也何弗
備之有哉禮者治之飾也治有未辯禮難乎具
矣必也神化之滲漉者蕩蕩乎措萬國于咸寧
夫然後五典敦焉五禮庸焉質文交濟品式詳
矣經綸有章幾微著矣蓋所以法天下傳後世
者在是而太平極治之規模可想也何弗具之
有哉吁觀先王有非常之治功而後有不世之
制作禮樂之道豈可以僞爲手抑治功急矣道
punctuated: 天而興，其建之爲功業者，有凝成之美矣。于是乎立樂以昭吾之功于不窮，雖文采節奏錯然異變也，孰非光烈之揄揚者乎？禮以節民之心，非强制也。蓋聖王嚮明而治，其敷之爲化理者，有底定之休矣。于是乎立禮以維吾之治于有常，雖制度文爲燦然異宜也，孰非經綸之顯設者乎？由是觀之，樂者，功之象也；功有未大，樂難乎備矣。必也宏動之掀揭者，巍巍乎冠百代而獨隆，夫然後九叙歌焉，九成舞焉，情文具舉，美善該矣，金王相宣，條理貫矣。蓋所以感天地、和神人者在是，而廣業崇功之氣象可挹也，何弗備之有哉？禮者，治之飾也；治有未辯，禮難乎具矣。必也神化之滲漉者，蕩蕩乎措萬國于咸寧，夫然後五典敦焉，五禮庸焉，質文交濟，品式詳矣，經綸有章，幾微著矣。蓋所以法天下、傳後世者在是，而太平極治之規模可想也，何弗具之有哉？吁！觀先王有非常之治功，而後有不世之制作，禮樂之道，豈可以僞爲手？抑治功急矣，道
translation_en: … rises at the height of heaven's favor, what he establishes as his achievements and enterprises possesses the beauty of solid completion. Thereupon he institutes music to manifest his achievements unendingly; although its embellishments and rhythms alternate in intricate variety, which of them is not an extolling of his glorious merit? Rites serve to regulate the minds of the people, and are not a matter of coercive restraint. For when a sage king faces the light to govern, what he spreads forth as transformative order possesses the blessing of settled stability. Thereupon he institutes rites to maintain his governance in constancy; although their statutes and ceremonial forms shine forth in varied appropriateness, which of them is not a manifest display of his statecraft? Viewed from this perspective, music is the emblem of achievement; if achievement is not yet great, it is difficult for music to be complete. Only when vast accomplishments [reading 勳 for 動] are held aloft, towering above a hundred generations in solitary magnificence—only then are the nine orders sung and the nine movements danced; sentiment and form are both upheld, beauty and goodness are both encompassed; metal and jade [reading 玉 for 王] resonate in turn, and coherent order runs through all. For that by which heaven and earth are moved and spirits and men are harmonized lies herein, and the grandeur of broad enterprise and exalted achievement can be beheld—how could anything be lacking in completeness? Rites are the adornment of governance; if governance is not yet pervasive, it is difficult for rites to be fully provided. Only when spiritual transformation permeates everywhere, vast and boundless, placing all the myriad states in universal peace—only then are the five cardinal relationships made笃 [earnest] and the five rites put into constant practice; substance and refinement complement each other, grades and models are detailed; statecraft has its patterns, and the subtlest springs of action are made manifest. For that by which a model is set for the world and transmitted to later generations lies herein, and the grand scale of supreme peace and ultimate order can be envisioned—how could anything be lacking in provision? Alas! Observing that the former kings first possessed extraordinary governance and achievement, and only afterward produced creations rare in any age, how could the Way of rites and music be forged by artifice [reading 乎 for 手]? Yet urgent as governance and achievement are, the Way…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
德尤要焉故觀罰招者思舜德論周官之法度
者必推本于關雎麟趾之意蓋禮樂之大原在
乎此彼煥焉可述者特其迹耳魯兩生謂禮樂
積德百年而後興漢臣亦曰天子建中和之極
旨哉言乎有志于制作者不可不深長思也
是故明君在上則諸臣服從
陳煒
同考試官知縣徐　批〔雄健之詞淵溢之趣〕
〔一洗繁冗而題意煥然文之絕佳者〕
===
考試官右中允何　批〔親切有味〕
考試官左中允范　批〔詞意精瑩必深于禮者〕
上有知臨之主而尊君之教達焉夫臣則君以
自治者也況乎明君臨之于上孰有不服從者
哉見于祭統者若曰教之立也有本而其從也
以身今君子之教外焉欲尊其君矣然豈徒責
之臣哉蓋必在上者亶聰明以作后而沉幾獨
運允協夫大君之宜全勇智以撫邦而峻德懋
昭克建夫維皇之極以熙庶績而濬哲之用昭
punctuated:
德尤要焉。故觀《罰招》者思舜德，論《周官》之法度者必推本于《關雎》、《麟趾》之意，蓋禮樂之大原在乎此；彼煥焉可述者，特其迹耳。魯兩生謂禮樂積德百年而後興，漢臣亦曰「天子建中和之極」，旨哉言乎！有志于制作者，不可不深長思也。

是故明君在上，則諸臣服從。
陳煒
同考試官知縣徐　批〔雄健之詞，淵溢之趣，〕〔一洗繁冗，而題意煥然，文之絕佳者。〕
考試官右中允何　批〔親切有味。〕
考試官左中允范　批〔詞意精瑩，必深于禮者。〕

上有知臨之主，而尊君之教達焉。夫臣則君以自治者也，況乎明君臨之于上，孰有不服從者哉？見于《祭統》者若曰：教之立也有本，而其從也以身。今君子之教，外焉欲尊其君矣，然豈徒責之臣哉？蓋必在上者，亶聰明以作后，而沉幾獨運，允協夫大君之宜；全勇智以撫邦，而峻德懋昭，克建夫維皇之極。以熙庶績，而濬哲之用昭，
translation_en:
… [moral] virtue is even more essential. Thus, those who observe the Shao music [罰招 for 韶招?] reflect upon the virtue of Shun, and those who discuss the institutions of the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan) must trace their roots back to the meaning of the "Guanju" and "Linzhi" odes. Indeed, the great source of rites and music lies herein; those brilliant things that can be recounted are merely their outward traces. The two scholars of Lu said that rites and music arise only after virtue has been accumulated for a hundred years, and a Han minister likewise said, "The Son of Heaven establishes the standard of equilibrium and harmony." How profound are these words! Those who aspire to institute rites and music cannot fail to ponder this deeply and at length.

"Therefore, when an enlightened ruler is above, all the ministers obey and follow."
Chen Wei 陳煒
Associate Examiner, District Magistrate Xu 徐 comments: [Vigorous diction and a deep, overflowing flair; it washes away prolixity so that the meaning of the theme shines forth brilliantly—an utterly superb essay.]
Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent He 何 comments: [Intimate and full of flavor.]
Examiner, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Fan 范 comments: [The diction and ideas are refined and lustrous; he must be someone deeply versed in the Classic of Rites.]

When above there is a sovereign who presides with wisdom, the teaching of honoring the ruler is achieved. Now, ministers pattern themselves after the ruler in order to govern themselves; how much more so when an enlightened ruler presides over them from above—who would not obey and follow? What appears in the "Summary of Sacrifices" ("Jitong") is as if to say: the establishment of teaching has its root, and compliance with it comes through personal example. Now, externally, the teaching of the noble man seeks to honor his ruler; yet how could this merely be demanded of the ministers? Truly, it must be that the one above is genuinely endowed with acute hearing and clear sight in acting as sovereign, and exercises profound foresight alone, truly harmonizing with what is fitting for a great ruler; and that he possesses complete courage and wisdom to pacify the state, while his lofty virtue shines brightly, enabling him to establish the august standard of the sovereign. In brightening the numerous achievements, the efficacy of his profound wisdom is made manifest; …

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
禮自我序焉樂自我和焉尊臨于五位而識周
乎萬徽所以爲羣辟之儀刑者此也以康四海
而文明之化溥德自我命焉罪自我討焉深居
乎九重而照加于萬里所以爲庶工之軌式者
此也有君如此而諸臣之服從也何如哉蓋其
履崇高之位在朝宁本有常尊而離照方中益
堅夫靖共之志當紀法之宗在臣下本有共仰
而大觀在上益動其翊戴之忱覩禮樂之明備
則曰吾君其日月乎何道之光也相與是訓是
===
行帖然祗奉之不暇非有所迫也惟聖憲天固
惟臣之所以欽若耳見命討之公平則曰吾君
其神明乎何燭之審也相與爲廉爲法肅然敬
應之不遑非有所强也元首惟明固股肱之所
以咸良耳夫以君之至明也待臣之術既盡而
臣之服從也尊君之敎遂生然則立敎者可不
知所本乎嘗觀堯舜在上則九官十二牧咸聚
于朝文武爲之君則四友十亂相與輔之當時
賛君德者曰知人則哲曰克知灼見可見君者
punctuated: 禮自我序焉，樂自我和焉，尊臨于五位而識周乎萬徽，所以爲羣辟之儀刑者此也；以康四海而文明之化溥，德自我命焉，罪自我討焉，深居乎九重而照加于萬里，所以爲庶工之軌式者此也。有君如此，而諸臣之服從也何如哉？蓋其履崇高之位，在朝宁本有常尊，而離照方中，益堅夫靖共之志；當紀法之宗，在臣下本有共仰，而大觀在上，益動其翊戴之忱。覩禮樂之明備，則曰：「吾君其日月乎！何道之光也！」相與是訓是行，帖然祗奉之不暇，非有所迫也；惟聖憲天，固惟臣之所以欽若耳。見命討之公平，則曰：「吾君其神明乎！何燭之審也！」相與爲廉爲法，肅然敬應之不遑，非有所强也；元首惟明，固股肱之所以咸良耳。夫以君之至明也，待臣之術既盡，而臣之服從也，尊君之敎遂生。然則立敎者，可不知所本乎？嘗觀堯、舜在上，則九官、十二牧咸聚于朝；文、武爲之君，則四友、十亂相與輔之。當時賛君德者，曰「知人則哲」，曰「克知灼見」。可見君者，
translation_en: … rites are ordered by him, and music is harmonized by him. Occupying the august position of the fifth line and extending his insight through all subtle signs, this is how he serves as a model for all the feudal lords. To bring peace to the Four Seas and spread the transforming influence of civilization, the virtuous are appointed by him, and the guilty are punished by him. Dwelling deep within the ninefold palace yet casting his illumination over ten thousand li, this is how he serves as a standard for all the officials. With a ruler such as this, how could all the ministers fail to submit and follow? Indeed, as he occupies the exalted position, he naturally commands constant reverence in the court; and when his radiant illumination is at its zenith, it further strengthens their resolve to quietly and恭敬ly fulfill their duties. Standing as the fountainhead of laws and regulations, he is naturally looked up to by all his subjects; and when his grand presence is above, it further stirs their sincere devotion to assist and support him. Witnessing the clarity and completeness of rites and music, they say: "Is our ruler not like the sun and the moon? How glorious is his Way!" Together they take his teachings as their guide and put them into practice, docilely and reverently upholding them without a moment to spare, not because anything compels them; it is simply that when the sage models himself on Heaven, his ministers naturally revere and accord with him. Seeing the fairness and impartiality of his appointments and punishments, they say: "Is our ruler not like the divine spirits? How discerning is his illumination!" Together they maintain integrity and abide by the law, solemnly and respectfully responding to him without leisure to tarry, not because anything forces them; it is simply that when the head is enlightened, the limbs are naturally all good. Thus, through the supreme enlightenment of the ruler, the art of treating ministers is fully realized, and through the submission and obedience of the ministers, the teaching of honoring the ruler naturally arises. This being so, how can one who establishes teaching not know its root? Looking back, when Yao and Shun were on the throne, the Nine Officials and Twelve Pastors all gathered at court; when King Wen and King Wu were rulers, the Four Friends and Ten Able Ministers joined in assisting them. Those who praised the ruler's virtue at the time said, "To know men is wisdom," and spoke of "truly knowing and clearly seeing." From this it can be seen that the ruler is…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
臣之標準明者君之要德此道也萬世所當法
也而祭獨具之故曰祭之爲物大矣
第貳場
論
人君先於虛己
江文明
同考試官學正黃　批　塲中作者類多浮冗
此篇發虛己納諫之義明白懇切而體格正大
辭意古雅是大有裨于君道者錄之不特以其
文而已
===
同考試官教授孫　批　人臣進言之時往往
以觸忌爲懼君人能曲體之則其心必虛而言
用矣子能以此立論深中肯綮而開闔抑揚精
思古調讀之爽然允宜高薦
考試官右中允何　批　發虛己爲受言之地懇切
明盡可占忠愛矣
考試官左中允范　批　發人君納諫之本意甚剴
切而詞復朗健眞可以式矣
punctuated:
臣之標準，明者君之要德。此道也，萬世所當法也，而祭獨具之，故曰：「祭之爲物大矣。」

第貳場
論
人君先於虛己
江文明
同考試官學正黃　批：塲中作者類多浮冗，此篇發虛己納諫之義，明白懇切，而體格正大，辭意古雅，是大有裨于君道者。錄之，不特以其文而已。
同考試官教授孫　批：人臣進言之時，往往以觸忌爲懼。君人能曲體之，則其心必虛而言用矣。子能以此立論，深中肯綮，而開闔抑揚，精思古調，讀之爽然，允宜高薦。
考試官右中允何　批：發虛己爲受言之地，懇切明盡，可占忠愛矣。
考試官左中允范　批：發人君納諫之本，意甚剴切，而詞復朗健，眞可以式矣。
translation_en:
… the standard for his ministers, and discernment is the essential virtue of a ruler. This Way is what ten thousand generations ought to take as their model, and the sacrifice alone embodies it; therefore it is said: "Great indeed is the sacrifice as an institution!"

Second Session
Discourse
"The Ruler of Men Puts Emptying Himself First"
Jiang Wenming

Associate Examiner Huang, Subprefectural Director of Studies, comments: Writers in the examination hall are mostly superficial and verbose. This essay brings out the meaning of emptying oneself to accept remonstrance clearly and earnestly, while its form and structure are upright and grand, and its diction and purport are classic and elegant. It is something of great benefit to the Way of the Ruler. We record it for publication not merely on account of its literary merit alone.

Associate Examiner Sun, Prefectural Director of Studies, comments: When ministers present their words, they often fear offending taboos. If one who rules over men can empathetically understand this in every detail, his mind will surely be open and their words will be adopted. You have been able to establish your discourse on this basis, hitting the crucial point deeply. Moreover, its opening and closing, its rising and falling cadence, its refined thought and ancient tone make for a refreshing read; it truly deserves a high recommendation.

Examiner He, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: It brings out how emptying oneself serves as the foundation for receiving advice, earnestly, clearly, and thoroughly; from this one may divine his loyalty and devotion to the sovereign.

Examiner Fan, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: It brings out the fundamental basis for a ruler's acceptance of remonstrance; the thought is extremely incisive and to the point, and the phrasing is furthermore clear and vigorous. It can truly serve as a model.

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人君所以能受天下之言者無他不以有己累
其心而已矣蓋所謂受言者非受之耳受之心
也心之弗虛言何繇入是故人君之心方翹然
有以自是而諫者顧矯其所是以明其非則�M
矣方訢然有以自便而諫者顧奪其所甚便而
投之以其所甚畏則拂矣何則有己之私足以
拒之也然則人君之德固莫盛於納諫而所以
爲納諫之本者又孰先於虛己哉請因羅豫章
之說而申之書不云乎嘉言罔攸伏而繼之曰
===
稽于衆舍己從人蓋人君之心必至於不恥稽
衆不難舍己而後嘉言有所自進苟惟己是賢
雖有嘉言將安用之在易有之山上有澤咸君
子以虛受人夫山澤之高下其勢邈然懸矣而
澤顧得以通氣於山者則山之虛受之也然則
人君處至尊之位而能盡下以開其言非虛其
誰受之夫心猶器然器虛而注之則挹滿則吐
矣是故明主必虛其心明主之心何心也無我
無人無內無外無左右無將迎無貴賤無戚疏
punctuated: 人君所以能受天下之言者，無他，不以有己累其心而已矣。蓋所謂受言者，非受之耳，受之心也。心之弗虛，言何繇入？是故人君之心，方翹然有以自是，而諫者顧矯其所是，以明其非，則M矣；方訢然有以自便，而諫者顧奪其所甚便，而投之以其所甚畏，則拂矣。何則？有己之私，足以拒之也。然則人君之德，固莫盛於納諫；而所以爲納諫之本者，又孰先於虛己哉？請因羅豫章之說而申之。《書》不云乎：「嘉言罔攸伏。」而繼之曰：「稽于衆，舍己從人。」蓋人君之心，必至於不恥稽衆，不難舍己，而後嘉言有所自進。苟惟己是賢，雖有嘉言，將安用之？在《易》有之：「山上有澤，咸。君子以虛受人。」夫山澤之高下，其勢邈然懸矣，而澤顧得以通氣於山者，則山之虛受之也。然則人君處至尊之位，而能盡下以開其言，非虛，其誰受之？夫心猶器然，器虛而注之則挹，滿則吐矣。是故明主必虛其心。明主之心，何心也？無我無人，無內無外，無左右，無將迎，無貴賤，無戚疏，
translation_en: The reason a ruler is able to accept the words of the world is none other than this: he simply does not encumber his mind with self-regard. For what is called accepting words is not accepting them with the ears, but accepting them with the mind. If the mind is not empty and open, how can words enter? Therefore, when a ruler’s mind is proudly convinced of its own rightness, and a remonstrator instead corrects what he deems right in order to expose his wrong, it will grate against [?] him; when he is delightedly indulging in his own convenience, and a remonstrator instead strips away what he finds most convenient and confronts him with what he most fears, he will be offended. Why is this? Because the selfishness of self-regard is enough to repel them. If so, among the virtues of a ruler, none is greater than accepting remonstrance; and as for the foundation of accepting remonstrance, what comes before emptying oneself? Allow me to elaborate on this on the basis of Luo Yuzhang’s (Luo Congyan 羅從彥) thesis. Does not the Book of Documents (Shu) say, “Good words are nowhere hidden”? And it continues by saying, “Consult with the multitude, set aside your own views and follow others.” Indeed, a ruler’s mind must reach the point where he is not ashamed to consult the multitude and does not find it difficult to set aside his own views, and only then will good words have a way to advance. If he regards only himself as worthy, even if there are good words, of what use will they be? In the Book of Changes (Yi) we find: “Above the mountain there is a marsh: Mutual Influence (Xian). The superior man thus receives others with openness.” Now, the height of a mountain and the lowness of a marsh are vastly separated in position, yet the marsh is able to communicate its vital breath with the mountain because the hollow openness of the mountain receives it. Thus, when a ruler occupies the position of supreme veneration and yet is able to exhaust the views of those below in order to open the way for their words—without an open mind, who could receive them? Now, the mind is like a vessel: when a vessel is empty and one pours into it, it takes it in; when it is full, it spills it out. Therefore, an enlightened ruler must empty his mind. What sort of mind is the mind of an enlightened ruler? It has neither self nor others, neither inside nor outside, neither left nor right, neither anticipation nor迎-welcoming bias, neither noble nor base, neither close kin nor distant, …

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
無衆寡無哲愚曠兮其若谷儼兮其若客兢兮
其若隊早兮其若抑能足以高一世而不敢以
能矜智足以鏡萬物而不敢以智炫威足以震
百辟而不敢以威逞勢足以極衆娛而不敢以
勢縱內而省躬則曰無逸志與外而考政則曰
無失節與億萬人至衆吾何以自奠安之億萬
里至遠吾何以自睹聽之歟然常有以自下聳
然常恐天下之不吾告此明主之心也由是則
不恃盛滿以忘規不諱危亡以嫉諫矣由是則
===
懇惻之論即能察其誠危激之談即能感其慮
矣由是則師保得以詔過卿士得以矯失工虞
瞽史何事非箴商旅庶人何言非法矣由是則
假之顏色猶恐其弗申厲之爵賞猶恐其弗奮
矣何哉蓋其心方切於求言而諫者之言與其
心適相契焉則其欣而受之也如渴者之於飲
饑者之於食也其悕而痞之也如矇者而濟之
視跂遠者而指之途也其獎直而貸其狂嘉忠
而寬其忤也如病者負痛於鍼石而不以爲毉
punctuated: 無衆寡，無哲愚。曠兮其若谷，儼兮其若客，兢兮其若隊，早兮其若抑。能足以高一世，而不敢以能矜；智足以鏡萬物，而不敢以智炫；威足以震百辟，而不敢以威逞；勢足以極衆娛，而不敢以勢縱。內而省躬，則曰：「無逸志與？」外而考政，則曰：「無失節與？億萬人至衆，吾何以自奠安之？億萬里至遠，吾何以自睹聽之？」歟然常有以自下，聳然常恐天下之不吾告。此明主之心也。由是，則不恃盛滿以忘規，不諱危亡以嫉諫矣；由是，則懇惻之論即能察其誠，危激之談即能感其慮矣；由是，則師保得以詔過，卿士得以矯失，工虞瞽史何事非箴？商旅庶人何言非法矣？由是，則假之顏色猶恐其弗申，厲之爵賞猶恐其弗奮矣。何哉？蓋其心方切於求言，而諫者之言與其心適相契焉。則其欣而受之也，如渴者之於飲，饑者之於食也；其悕而痞之也，如矇者而濟之視，跂遠者而指之途也；其獎直而貸其狂，嘉忠而寬其忤也，如病者負痛於鍼石，而不以爲毉
translation_en:
…free of distinctions between many and few, or between wise and foolish. Vast, it is like a valley; solemn, it is like a guest; cautious, it is as if about to fall; humble [?], it is as if restrained. Though his ability suffices to surpass a whole generation, he dares not boast of his ability; though his wisdom suffices to mirror the myriad things, he dares not flaunt his wisdom; though his majesty suffices to awe the hundred officials, he dares not indulge his majesty; though his power suffices to exhaust every pleasure, he dares not give rein to his power. Inwardly examining himself, he says, "Have I no dissolute intentions?" Outwardly reviewing his governance, he says, "Have I no lapses in measure? The hundreds of millions of people are most numerous—how can I by myself settle and bring them peace? The hundreds of millions of li are most distant—how can I by myself see and hear them all?" Modestly [?], he always keeps himself humble; alertly, he always fears that the world will not inform him. Such is the mind of an enlightened ruler.

Because of this, he will not rely on fullness and prosperity to forget admonition, nor shun talk of peril and ruin to resent remonstrance. Because of this, upon hearing earnest and heartfelt arguments he can immediately perceive their sincerity, and upon hearing alarming and impassioned words he can immediately be moved by their concern. Because of this, Preceptors and Guardians are able to告 advise him of faults, Ministers and Gentlemen are able to rectify his errors—among artisans, foresters, blind musicians, and scribes, what affair is not an admonition? Among merchants, travelers, and commoners, what word is not a model? Because of this, even when granting them a warm countenance he still fears they will not speak out fully, and even when encouraging them with noble ranks and rewards he still fears they will not rouse themselves.

Why is this? It is because his mind is earnestly set upon seeking counsel, and the words of the remonstrators happen to tally with his own mind. Thus his joyful acceptance of them is like a thirsty man coming to drink, or a hungry man coming to food; his cherishing and relying [?] upon them is like aiding a blind man with sight, or pointing out the road to one straining to reach afar; his rewarding of candor while pardoning rashness, and commending of loyalty while forgiving offense, is like a sick man enduring the pain of acupuncture needles and stone probes without blaming the physician…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
讓也如此則何言之不可擇何諫之不可受乎
蓋古之稱受言者莫過於禹一饋十起建鼓縣
鐸以求天下之言而一聞昌言則亟拜焉當是
時羣臣之賢豈有可補於禹乃詘巳受言恒若
弗逮胡若是急也及觀史氏之紀其德也曰不
矜曰不伐曰不自滿假其會同也則問於諸侯
曰諸侯以寡人爲驕乎其朔日朝也則問於士
然後知禹之所以能受言者是心爲之也微獨
===
大禹昔者軒轅氏之有天下也受學於王屋諏
道於崆峒登具茨而師大隗隮岱宗而奉中黃
推步洛力牧占候詢山稽舜命九官各比其職
明目達聰詢岳洛牧又何若是汲汲也夫軒轅
氏生而能言卽役使百靈有虞氏握璣衡懷神
珠史稱濬哲文明其道豈在山稽力牧之下而
智顧不若二十有二人哉誠懼夫心之不虛則
無以捐蹠盭之知而建會通之節撤愼忮之明
以蹐昭曠之路爾故曰天道虧盈而益謙地道
punctuated: 讓也。如此，則何言之不可擇，何諫之不可受乎？蓋古之稱受言者莫過於禹。一饋十起，建鼓縣鐸，以求天下之言，而一聞昌言，則亟拜焉。當是時，羣臣之賢豈有可補於禹？乃詘巳受言，恒若弗逮，胡若是急也？及觀史氏之紀其德也，曰不矜，曰不伐，曰不自滿假。其會同也，則問於諸侯曰：「諸侯以寡人爲驕乎？」其朔日朝也，則問於士。然後知禹之所以能受言者，是心爲之也。微獨大禹，昔者軒轅氏之有天下也，受學於王屋，諏道於崆峒，登具茨而師大隗，隮岱宗而奉中黃，推步洛力牧，占候詢山稽。舜命九官，各比其職，明目達聰，詢岳洛牧，又何若是汲汲也？夫軒轅氏生而能言，卽役使百靈；有虞氏握璣衡，懷神珠，史稱「濬哲文明」。其道豈在山稽、力牧之下，而智顧不若二十有二人哉？誠懼夫心之不虛，則無以捐蹠盭之知而建會通之節，撤愼忮之明以蹐昭曠之路爾。故曰：「天道虧盈而益謙，地道…
translation_en: …for blame. When it is like this, what words cannot be selected, and what remonstrances cannot be accepted? Indeed, among the ancients renowned for accepting counsel, none surpassed Yu 禹. During a single meal he rose ten times, and he set up drums and hung bells with wooden clappers in order to seek the words of the world; and as soon as he heardsplendid words of counsel, he promptly bowed to them. At that time, how could the worthiness of the assembled ministers have anything to add to Yu? Yet he humbled himself to accept their words, constantly as though he could not catch up—why was he in such haste? When one examines the historians' record of his virtue, it says he was "not boastful," "not bragging," and "not self-satisfied or presumptuous." When he held grand audiences with the feudal lords, he would ask them, "Do the feudal lords consider me arrogant?" And when he held court on the first day of the month, he would question the officers. Only then does one know that the reason Yu was able to accept counsel was that this mind of his made it so. And it was not only Great Yu. In antiquity, when Xuan-yuan 軒轅氏 [the Yellow Emperor] possessed the world, he received instruction at Mount Wangwu 王屋, inquired into the Way at Mount Kongtong 崆峒, ascended Mount Juci 具茨 to take Dawei 大隗 as his master, climbed Mount Daizong 岱宗 [Mount Tai] to revere Zhonghuang 中黃, consulted [?] Limu 力牧 on calendrical calculations, and inquired of Shanji 山稽 on astrological prognostication. Shun 舜 charged the Nine Officials, each harmonizing with his duty, and to see clearly and hear distinctly, he inquired of the Four Peaks and consulted [?] the Pastors—why were they also so tirelessly urgent? Now, Xuan-yuan could speak from birth and forthwith commanded the hundred spirits; the Lord of Yu 有虞氏 [Shun] grasped the armillary sphere and cherished the divine pearl, and the histories praised him as "profoundly wise, cultured, and bright." How could their Way have been inferior to that of Shanji and Limu, or their wisdom less than that of the twenty-two men? Truly, they feared that if the mind is not receptive and empty, there would be no way to cast aside perverse and crooked cleverness so as to establish the standard of comprehensive accommodation, or to remove guarded and jealous acuity [?] so as to tread the bright and spacious road. Therefore it is said: "The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and augments the humble; the Way of Earth…"

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
變盈而流謙謙者虛也虛者盈之反也夫人君
之所居至尊貴也所享至愉佚也況其心有所
未虛而以自矜自用之意概於其中則又何取
於諫者之說而疆受之故與之論大道則見以
爲闊事情與之謫細過則見以爲彰主失拙訥
其辭則見以爲淺略而寡智廣肆其說則見以
爲草野而倨侮於是有惡聞乎强諍如尤左儒
之別君者矣有耻屈於正論如憾魏徵之辱巳
者矣有騁辯以折人之言如發十策以難弘者
===
矣有役智以逆人之情如揣公輔爲賣直者矣
夫德宗之猜愎姑置勿論乃三君者皆有絶人
之賢高世之智而猶若是直其心自賢智爾人
主一有自賢智之心則恃長矜巳雖周旦召奭
無所售其悃矣疆遂而辯雖孔丘孟軻無所殫
其論矣設爲叵測以赫然臨之雖龍逄比干無
所關其忠矣若然則讜議不聞而國是日非是
自賢智之過也彼賢智之君當其矯情以從善
也諫者亦得以伸其說及其私意溺而本眞露
punctuated: 變盈而流謙。」謙者，虛也；虛者，盈之反也。夫人君之所居，至尊貴也；所享，至愉佚也。況其心有所未虛，而以自矜自用之意概於其中，則又何取於諫者之說而疆受之？故與之論大道，則見以爲闊事情；與之謫細過，則見以爲彰主失；拙訥其辭，則見以爲淺略而寡智；廣肆其說，則見以爲草野而倨侮。於是有惡聞乎强諍，如尤左儒之別君者矣；有耻屈於正論，如憾魏徵之辱巳者矣；有騁辯以折人之言，如發十策以難弘者矣；有役智以逆人之情，如揣公輔爲賣直者矣。夫德宗之猜愎，姑置勿論；乃三君者，皆有絶人之賢、高世之智，而猶若是，直其心自賢智爾。人主一有自賢智之心，則恃長矜巳，雖周旦、召奭無所售其悃矣；疆遂而辯，雖孔丘、孟軻無所殫其論矣；設爲叵測以赫然臨之，雖龍逄、比干無所關其忠矣。若然，則讜議不聞而國是日非，是自賢智之過也。彼賢智之君，當其矯情以從善也，諫者亦得以伸其說；及其私意溺而本眞露
translation_en: …alters the full and flows toward the humble." Humility is emptiness of self, and emptiness is the opposite of fullness. Now, the position a ruler occupies is supremely noble and exalted, and what he enjoys is supremely pleasant and comfortable. Moreover, if his mind is not yet empty of self, and a spirit of self-conceit and self-will fills it within, what would he find to value in the words of remonstrators that he should force himself to accept them? Therefore, if one discusses the Great Way with him, it is viewed as detached from practical realities; if one faults minor errors with him, it is viewed as exposing the sovereign's failings; if one's words are plain and halting, it is viewed as shallow, sketchy, and lacking in wisdom; if one expands freely upon one's arguments, it is viewed as rustic and insolent. Thus there have been those who hated hearing forceful remonstrance, like blaming Zuo Ru (左儒) for siding against his ruler; those who were ashamed to yield to upright arguments, like resenting Wei Zheng (魏徵) for humiliating him; those who gave free rein to sophistry to refute others' words, like issuing ten policy questions to stump Gongsun Hong (公孫弘); and those who employed cleverness to suspect others' motives, like surmising that Jiang Gongfu (姜公輔) was peddling uprightness for fame. Now, let us leave aside without discussion the suspicious obstinacy of Emperor Dezong (德宗) of Tang; yet the other three rulers all possessed surpassing worthiness and wisdom lofty above their age, and still they acted like this simply because in their minds they considered themselves worthy and wise. Once a ruler has a mind that considers itself worthy and wise, he relies on his strengths and boasts of himself, so that even Dan, Duke of Zhou (周旦), and Shi, Duke of Shao (召奭), would have no way to offer their sincere devotion; he stubbornly persists and argues back, so that even Kong Qiu (孔丘, Confucius) and Meng Ke (孟軻, Mencius) would have no way to set forth their discourses in full; he puts on an unfathomable air and confronts them with intimidating wrath, so that even Guan LongA (關龍逄) and Bigan (比干) would have no way to present their loyalty. If it is like this, then honest counsel goes unheard and state policy grows daily more perverse; this is the fault of considering oneself worthy and wise. With those worthy and wise rulers, when they restrain their inclinations to follow the good, remonstrators are able to advance their views; but when they become immersed in selfish intentions and their true nature is exposed…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也則往往咈諫之失見焉何也其心盈也盈則
實實則中距者堅中距者堅則外傳者解體矣
夫心有虛實則言有聽距此在明君然矣而况
餘主哉故曰納諫要矣虛已急焉此之謂也然
不獨納諫之本於虛已也而欲開諫者路也亦
莫切乎是蓋人君之心羣臣之所伺以爲避就
者也矧諫爭之事觸忌以申詞蒙死而竭智爲
臣者義之所激無不欲犯顏苦口爲主上一言
而迴思却慮其閑喙而休投牘而廢者多矣人
===
君方師心自任而以訑訑示天下則彼亦何樂
於冒主上之所不願聽者而賈其罪也故上有
少嚴之色則下萌傾旨之心上有微譴之辭則
下起避辜之念意指一異而觀望者衆矣人君
可不思虛已以導之邪是以古之明君懸旒蔽
目垂纊塞耳而其臨羣臣也自稱寡德不穀蓋
懼聰明才智之或見而人之有聰明才智者皆
退焉莫敢爲我盡也嗚呼其知來諫之道也哉
表
punctuated:
也，則往往咈諫之失見焉。何也？其心盈也。盈則實，實則中距者堅，中距者堅則外傳者解體矣。夫心有虛實，則言有聽距，此在明君然矣，而况餘主哉？故曰：「納諫要矣，虛已急焉」，此之謂也。然不獨納諫之本於虛已也，而欲開諫者路也，亦莫切乎是。蓋人君之心，羣臣之所伺以爲避就者也。矧諫爭之事，觸忌以申詞，蒙死而竭智。爲臣者，義之所激，無不欲犯顏苦口爲主上一言；而迴思却慮，其閑喙而休、投牘而廢者多矣。人君方師心自任，而以訑訑示天下，則彼亦何樂於冒主上之所不願聽者，而賈其罪也？故上有少嚴之色，則下萌傾旨之心；上有微譴之辭，則下起避辜之念。意指一異，而觀望者衆矣，人君可不思虛已以導之邪？是以古之明君，懸旒蔽目，垂纊塞耳，而其臨羣臣也，自稱「寡德」、「不穀」，蓋懼聰明才智之或見，而人之有聰明才智者皆退焉莫敢爲我盡也。嗚呼！其知來諫之道也哉！

表
translation_en:
… the fault of defying remonstrance often appears. Why is this? Because their minds are full of themselves. When full, they are closed off; when closed off, internal resistance grows firm; and when internal resistance is firm, those who would convey counsel from the outside lose heart. Whether the mind is open or closed determines whether words are heeded or rejected—if this is true even of enlightened rulers, how much more so of other sovereigns! Therefore it is said: "Accepting remonstrance is important, but humbling oneself is urgent." This is what is meant. Yet humbling oneself is not only the foundation of accepting remonstrance; if one wishes to open the path for remonstrators, nothing is more vital than this. For the mind of the ruler is what all the ministers watch closely in deciding what to avoid and what to pursue. How much more so in the matter of remonstrance and contention, where one braves taboos to present one's words and risks death to exhaust one's wisdom! Among ministers, stirred by righteousness, there are none who do not wish to brave the imperial countenance and speak bitter truths in offering a word for their sovereign; yet upon turning the matter over in their minds and shrinking back in apprehension, many are those who hold their tongues and desist, or cast aside their memorials and give up. If the ruler is just then relying on his own judgment and displaying self-satisfied arrogance to the world, what pleasure would they take in braving what their sovereign is unwilling to hear only to invite punishment upon themselves? Thus, when the superior shows a slightly stern countenance, inferiors conceive the desire to cater to his wishes; when the superior utters a mildly reprimanding word, inferiors give rise to the thought of evading blame. Once the ruler's inclination shifts ever so slightly, those who wait and watch in hesitation become numerous. How can a ruler not think of humbling himself in order to guide them to speak? Therefore, the enlightened rulers of antiquity hung jade pendants from their crowns to veil their eyes and suspended floss silk to plug their ears, and when they presided over their assembled ministers, they referred to themselves as "Of Scant Virtue" or "Unworthy." This was because they feared that if their own acuity, intelligence, talent, and wisdom were to be displayed, then others possessing acuity, intelligence, talent, and wisdom would all retreat and not dare to exhaust their efforts on the ruler's behalf. Alas! Truly they understood the Way of inviting remonstrance!

Memorials

translation_en:
An Imitation Memorial of Gratitude by Wang Zeng 王曾 [written as 王㑹] of the Song Dynasty, on Selecting and Recording Sixty Deeds of Ancient Sages and Worthies and Presenting Them with Illustrations, Upon Which the Emperor Issued an Edict of Praise, Ordered the Palace Agency to Present Twenty Scrolls Monthly, and Further Ordered Blocks Engraved to Print and Bestow Them upon Close Ministers (First Year of Tiansheng [1023]).

By Fang Yingxuan 方應選.

Associate Examiner, Instructor Ou 區, comments: "This topic reveals a worthy minister offering loyalty and a brilliant ruler accepting counsel at that time—a flourishing of mutual accord eminently worthy of record. Whereas writers in the examination hall mostly resorted to plagiarism and superficiality, this piece alone achieves comprehensive coherence and clear incisiveness. Moreover, its diction is classic, elegant, fresh, and striking, expressing a subject's loyalty and devotion to the fullest. Is it merely skillful in parallel prose (siliu)? It may serve as a model."

Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Zhu 諸, comments: "The exposition is clear and incisive, suffused with loyalty and devotion…" [Note: line repeated across leaf fold]
Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Zhu 諸, comments: "The exposition is clear and incisive, suffused with loyalty and devotion. It is not merely skillful in parallel elegance; it truly deserves a high recommendation."

Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Long 龍, comments: "Dignified and canonical in standard; not the work of one who merely crafts words and phrases. It should be recorded as a model."

Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent He 何, comments: "Detailed, nuanced, and earnest—not merely skillful in parallel prose. Selected."

Examiner, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Fan 范, comments: "Elegant in parallelism and canonical in standard, suffused with the spirit of loyalty and devotion. It deserves to stand first among the many scholars."

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
皇上沖年御寓竊效愚忠詮錄古先聖賢事蹟
凡六十事繪圖以
獻伏蒙
聖明嘉納降
詔褒美
命禁署月進二十軸仍鏤版摹印遍
賜近臣臣曾誠懽誠忭稽首頓首稱
謝者
聖垂懿範恭依繪事以陳謨
===
帝受昌言寵被
綸音而示獎王檢程分于
禁禦琅函侈
錫于臣隣徵
畜德之日新宜豫鳴之雷動祈而且謝頌敢
忘規竊惟聖賢爲道法之宗人王建皇彝
之極心以鑑而知古德由盤而可新故夫
圖畫之興亦與簡書並遠史皇作而盡物
象軒后受以紀人倫亳宮攡九主之儀式
punctuated:
皇上沖年御寓，竊效愚忠，詮錄古先聖賢事蹟凡六十事，繪圖以獻。伏蒙聖明嘉納，降詔褒美，命禁署月進二十軸，仍鏤版摹印，遍賜近臣。臣曾誠懽誠忭，稽首頓首稱謝者：
聖垂懿範，恭依繪事以陳謨；帝受昌言，寵被綸音而示獎。王檢程分于禁禦，琅函侈錫于臣隣。徵畜德之日新，宜豫鳴之雷動。祈而且謝，頌敢忘規？竊惟聖賢爲道法之宗，人王建皇彝之極。心以鑑而知古，德由盤而可新。故夫圖畫之興，亦與簡書並遠。史皇作而盡物象，軒后受以紀人倫。亳宮攡九主之儀，式…
translation_en:
…His Majesty assuming rule over the realm in his tender years, privately offered up my humble loyalty by selecting and recording the deeds of ancient sages and worthies—sixty episodes in all—and illustrating them in paintings to present to the throne. I have humbly received Your Sacred Sight's gracious acceptance, the issuance of an imperial edict of praise, and the command that the palace offices submit twenty scrolls each month, while also carving woodblocks to print copies for wide bestowal upon the close ministers. Your servant [Wang] Zeng, truly joyful and truly elated, bows his head to the ground and offers thanks:

The sages handed down admirable models, and I respectfully relied on the art of painting to set forth counsels; the Emperor accepted flourishing words, and I was favored with silken imperial pronouncements that displayed encouragement. Jade-clasped scrolls are scheduled for presentation by installment within the palace precincts, and precious cases are generously bestowed upon the minister-attendants. This attests to the daily renewal of Your cultivated virtue, and fittingly calls forth joyful acclamation resounding like thunder. Praying for blessings while offering thanks, in my eulogy how dare I forget admonition?

I humbly reflect that the sages and worthies are the ancestors of the Way and its laws, and the ruler of men establishes the supreme standard of august norms. The mind, by taking a mirror, comes to know antiquity; virtue, through the inscription on the washbasin, can be renewed. Therefore, the rise of pictorial illustration is just as ancient as that of bamboo slips and books. Shi Huang [Cangjie] created it to exhaust the forms of things, and the Sovereign轩 [the Yellow Emperor] received it to record human relationships. In the palace at Bo were displayed the models of the Nine Rulers, thereby…

title: 萬曆元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
著保衡之訓周灝絺四墉之狀爰昭篤棐
之猷蓋書雖盡意意盡言故章施是設而事
以不尊不信則聖哲爲徵獻忠比于韋弦
懋德資其斧藻托契攸在振古如斯若乃
宋弘座障之規義存好德班伯畫屏之諫
志在繩愆璟慕無逸于內庭文績尚書于
太液彼雖洵美終乏兼資〔臣初〕誦讀之時
